text.p: These are leading stories in this morning's Paris newspapers.

-- Industry Minister Franck Borotra against plans by Renault and Peugeot carmakers to rejuvenate their workforce if there would not also be an industrial project. He says government opposes financing layoffs, favours industrial cooperation to improve competitivity.
-- High cost expected for insurance companies after fire broke on a lorry aboard a Eurotunnel shuttle yesterday, causing serious damage to the tunnel, which is expected to reopen in two weeks.

-- President Jacques Chirac during state visit to Japan reaffirms will go ahead with current austerity policy despite its negative impact on opinion, admits policy could have been better explained to the French.

-- European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy in an interview insists on necessary stability for the future european currency, which he sees as gradually taking a role comparable to that of the dollar.
-- Euro Disney posts a 77 percent rise in profit for year to Sept 30.
-- Lorry drivers persist in strike and demonstrations for better working conditions, block roads throughout France.

-- OFCE study sees number of jobseekers growing by 40,000 to 50,000 a year through 2001, accompanied by sluggish consumption and a 1 percent rise in mandatory payroll social security contributions by 1998 due to low earnings.
-- GAN chairman Jean-Jacques Bonnaud refuses to bow to government's dismissal, denies having blocked privatisation process of subsidiary CIC.

-- A Thomson Multimedia (TMM) workers' association says that if a Daewoo Electronics offer to take over TMM as part of Thomson privatisation is accepted, Daewoo will receive some 250 million dollars a year from licences currently held by General Electric and expected to be returned to TMM from 1999.
-- National Assembly to look at bill on pension funds tomorrow, amended to include a maximum of 20 percent for lump sum withdrawals.
-- One factor for economic pickup in 1997 may be an expected rise in the price of commodities, study shows.
-- Euro Disney profits rocket 76 percent, but increasing debt interest payment and royalty payments to the Walt Disney Company from 1998 weigh on the company's outlook.
